blocks.text: **Dynamic programming (DP)** is a way to solve problems that break into **smaller problems of the same kind** — like recursion — when those smaller problems **repeat**. Instead of solving the same one again and again, you solve each one **once**, store its answer, and look it up every time it's needed again. That single idea turns many exponential searches into fast, polynomial-time algorithms.

blocks.alt: The call tree of a plain recursive fib(5) has 15 calls. fib(3) is computed twice and fib(2) three times; the orange nodes are repeated work. Dynamic programming computes each of fib(0) to fib(5) exactly once, left to right: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 — six steps instead of fifteen calls.

blocks.text: A problem can be solved with DP when it has both of these:

items: **Overlapping subproblems** — a recursive solution asks the same smaller question many times. fib(5) needs fib(3) twice; a grid path count needs the count from the same cell over and over. (Merge sort splits into subproblems too, but they never repeat — that's plain divide and conquer, not DP.)

**Optimal substructure** — the answer to the big problem is built from the answers to smaller problems. The cheapest way up a staircase ends with the cheapest way to one of the two steps below; the longest common subsequence of two strings comes from the LCS of their shorter prefixes.

blocks.text: From recursion to DP: three steps
Almost every DP solution grows from a plain recursion, and you'll see these three versions in every lesson of this course:

items: **1. Plain recursion** — write the recurrence directly. Correct but exponential, because it re-solves the overlapping subproblems.
**2. Memoization (top-down)** — the same recursion, plus a cache: before computing a subproblem, check whether it's been solved. Next lesson.

**3. Tabulation (bottom-up)** — skip the recursion: fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward, in an order where everything a cell needs is already filled. Often followed by **saving memory** — keeping only the part of the table still needed.

blocks.caption: The plain recursion: watch how often the same small calls come back.

blocks.text: DP's running time is simple to count: **the number of distinct subproblems × the work to solve one** (given the answers to the smaller ones). Fibonacci has n + 1 subproblems, each one addition: O(n), instead of about 1.6ⁿ calls. The memory is the size of the table — unless you shrink it, which the fourth lesson shows.

blocks.code:
problem                      subproblems        work each     time
Fibonacci                    n                  O(1)          O(n)
Climbing stairs              n                  O(1)          O(n)
Unique paths in a grid       m × n              O(1)          O(m · n)
Longest common subsequence   m × n              O(1)          O(m · n)
Coin change (amount A)       A                  O(coins)      O(A · coins)
Longest increasing subseq.   n                  O(n)          O(n²)

blocks.text: How to recognise a DP problem

items: It asks for a **count** (how many ways), an **optimum** (minimum cost, maximum profit, longest, shortest) or a **yes/no** (can it be done?) — not for a list of every solution (that's backtracking).
It's described as a **sequence of decisions**: take or skip, step one or two, match or edit a letter.
A brute-force recursion is easy to write but **times out**, because the same state comes up again and again.
The constraints are moderate: n up to a few thousand for O(n²), up to 10⁵ or 10⁶ for O(n).
DP = recursion + **remembering** answers to repeated subproblems.
Time = number of states × work per state; memory = the table (often shrinkable).
Write the plain recursion first, then memoize it, then turn it into a table.
